div.p: The analysis of global multiprocessor scheduling is more difficult than its uniprocessor counterpart. Due to the unknown critical instant, existing techniques use overapproximations of task interference for efficient yet pessimistic analysis. In this paper, we proposed a new technique to improve the precision of interference estimation. The key is to identify and resolve contradicting assumptions made in the analysis procedure. The resulting new analysis method improves the analysis precision at the price of a higher complexity. Then we introduce techniques to optimize the new method for better efficiency. Experiments with randomly generated task sets are conducted to evaluate both the precision and efficiency of the proposed new method.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: It is widely accepted that future real-time embedded systems will be deployed on multi-core processors, to meet their rapidly increasing requirements of both high computational capacity and low power consumption. Multiprocessor scheduling is one of the fundamental problems in the design of efficient multi-core real-time systems. This problem has drawn tremendous interest in the real-time system research community in recent years.

Multiprocessor scheduling is usually categorized into two paradigms [15]: global scheduling, in which each task can execute on any available processor at run time, and partitioned scheduling in which each task is assigned to a processor beforehand, and at run time each task can only execute on this particular processor. For partitioned scheduling, the schedulability analysis problem is reduced to the uniprocessor form and the challenge is how to do taskprocessor assignment for better resource utilization (which is similar to the bin-packing problem). By contrast, the analysis of global scheduling is fundamentally different from and significantly more difficult than analyzing uniprocessor scheduling [9]. In this paper, we focus on the analysis of global scheduling, and in particular we consider the preemptive fixed-priority global scheduling algorithm.

The difficulty of analyzing global scheduling lies in the fact that the critical instant in global scheduling is in general unknown. Several attempts have been made to exhaustively analyze global scheduling by either explicit or symbolic state space enumeration [20], [21], [6], but all run into serious scalability problems. To handle reallife size systems, people resort to over-approximate analysis techniques that are efficient but pessimistic. The basic idea of these techniques is to derive an upper bound of the interference contributed by each individual task, and use the sum of individual tasks' upper bounds to bound the total interference of the system. An important concept here is the so-called carry-in, which is the workload of an interfering task that is released before but may execute in the busy period. To safely bound the maximal interference of each individual task, one should assume that interference contributed by carry-in of each task is as large as possible. However, the conditions that lead to the worst-case carryin of individual tasks may contradict with each other from a system-level perspective. Therefore, it is possible to utilize system-level information to exclude behaviors that are impossible at runtime, and thus improve the precision of carry-in interference estimations. Several techniques have been proposed to reduce pessimism in carry-in estimation [5], [19], [7], [9], [22], [10]. The state-of-the-art analysis method for global fixed-priority scheduling is GSYY [22], which outperforms previous methods by limiting the total number of tasks that can introduce carry-in into the busy period.

In this paper, we present a new analysis method for global fixed-priority scheduling, which further improves the carryin interference estimation precision over the state-of-the-art method GSYY. The key observation of our new method is as follows. In GSYY, the carry-in of an interfering task is maximized under the assumption that other processors are idle when the carry-in is executed. On the other hand, however, the carry-in is counted into the interference to the analyzed task under the assumption that other processors are busy when the carry-in is executed. These two assumptions contradict with each other, which means the abstraction used in GSYY includes impossible system behaviors that lead to pessimistic analysis results. The major contribution of our new analysis method is to partially address the above contradiction, exclude impossible system behaviors from the abstraction domain, and consequently improve the analysis precision. The improved precision is at the price of higher complexity. We also introduce optimizations to improve the efficiency of the new method.

We conduct experiments with randomly generated task systems to evaluate our new methods. Experimental results show that our new method gives non-trivial improvement in analysis precision compared with the state-of-the-art method GSYY. We also evaluate the analysis efficiency of our new method. It is shown that with the presented optimization techniques our new method can handle large-scale task systems in very short time.

div.head: A. Related Work
div.p: Global multiprocessor scheduling algorithms based on uniprocessor scheduling algorithms like RM and EDF suffer from the so-called Dhall effect [18], namely some system with utilization arbitrarily close to 1 can be not schedulable no matter how many processors are added to the system. This result has a big influence on the view of global scheduling. Over a long time, global scheduling has been considered to be unsuitable for real-time systems. One way to overcome the Dhall effect is fairness scheduling [11], which splits up the task's execution into small pieces and interleaves them with other tasks, to keep the execution of a task to progress in the speed proportional to its workload. Fairness scheduling and its variants [3], [1], [2] can achieve optimality in many cases, but incur large runtime overheads.

In [4] it is shown that the Dhall effect is mainly a problem with high-utilization tasks and can be effectively compensated by increasing processor speed (rather than adding processors). The major obstacle in precisely analyzing global scheduling is the unknown critical instant. Several attempts have been made to exhaustively analyze global scheduling by either explicit or symbolic state space enumeration [20], [21], [6], but all run into serious scalability problem. A large body of works have been done in efficient analysis of global scheduling by over-approximation. Baker [5] proposed the problem window analysis framework, which first calculates an upper bound of the workload contributed by each individual task, then uses the sum of the upper bound of each individual task as upper bound of the total workload of the task system. One key contribution in Baker's analysis is to bound the ratio of the carry-in job's workload that actually causes interference. Later, Bertogna et al. [13], [14] observed that the workload in parallel with the analyzed job do not need to be accounted into its interference, and provided a new test condition of polynomial time-complexity, which in many cases outperforms Baker's analysis. Baruah [9] introduced the busy-period concept for the analysis of global EDF scheduling, which limits the number of tasks that have carryin to be M -1, where M is the number of processors. This can significantly improve the analysis precision, at the price of higher complexity due to enumerating possible lengths of the busy period. Bertogna and Cirinei [12] explored task slack time with response time analysis to reduce over-estimation of carry-in of each task. Guan et al [22] combined the techniques in [9] and [12], and observed that the limited carry-in technique in [9] comes for free in the analysis of global fixed-priority scheduling, i.e., can greatly improve its precision over [12] without lowering the analysis efficiency. This leads to an abstract form of the critical instant. Later it is proved by Davis and Burns [17] that this abstract critical instant is not a property specific to the analysis in [22], but rather a general property of global fixed-priority scheduling itself. The limited carry-in technique has been applied to a wider range of scheduling algorithms, namely work-conserving multiprocessor scheduling algorithms [23], [25]. Several analysis methods [19], [7], [8] for global fixed-priority scheduling are proposed, with the main target of better resource augmentation bounds. Although these analysis methods can provide good quantitative performance guarantees in the worst-case, they are typically less precise than GSYY in analyzing concrete task systems.

div.head: B. Organization
div.p: The remaining of the paper is organized as follows.

Section II defines the system model and the problem to be solved. In Section III we review the state-of-the-art analysis method and identify its pessimism and the opportunity for our improvement. Our new analysis method is presented in Section IV, and experimental evaluation is conducted in Section V. Finally, Section VI concludes the paper.

div.head: II. PROBLEM SETTING
div.p: We consider a task set τ consisting of N sporadic tasks which are executing upon a multiprocessor platform of M processors. A task is represented by a triple τ i = (C i , T i , D i ), where C i is the worst-case execution time (WCET), D i is the relative deadline and T i is the period (the minimum interval between two successive released jobs) of the task, respectively. We assume that all tasks have constrained deadlines, i.e., D i ≤ T i for each task τ i .
We use U i = Ci Ti to denote the utilization of task τ i . U = N i=1 U i is the total utilization of the task set, and U = U/M is the normalized total utilization of the task set.

Every task releases an infinite sequence of jobs at runtime. The j th job of task τ i is denoted by J j i , where r j i is the release time of J j i and f j i is its finish time. Moreover, d j i = r j i + D i is the absolute deadline of J j i . We also use J i to denote a job of task τ i when it is clear from the context which job of τ i we are referring to, and use r i , f i and d i to denote its release time, finish time and absolute deadline, respectively.

In fixed-priority scheduling, the priority of a task is statically assigned and all jobs generated by this task inherit this priority. We assume tasks are sorted by priority from high to low, i.e., i < j implies the priority of task τ i is higher than τ j .

The problem to solve is to analyze the worst-case response time of each task. We use R j i = f j i -r j i to denote the response time of a job J j i of task τ i , The worst-case response time of a task is the maximum among the response times of all its released jobs. Since precise worst-case response time analysis is intractable, we aim to derive a safe upper bound of the response time of all jobs released by a task.

A task is schedulable iff R i ≤ D i , and the task set is schedulable iff all tasks are schedulable. Besides used for checking the schedulability, the WCRT of a task itself is also of interests in many applications, such as in the distributed systems where the finishing of a task decides the release of some task in the downstream processing/communication unit.
For simplicity of expression, we further use the following notations to express that a value A is "limited" if it is below or above a certain threshold B or C, respectively:

div.head: III. PESSIMISM IN STATE-OF-THE-ART METHOD
div.p: Before presenting our new method, we provide a brief review of the state-of-the-art analysis method GSYY [22] and identify its pessimism.

div.head: A. Review of GSYY
div.p: In our problem model, the behavior of a task is not affected by lower-priority tasks, so the analysis of each task can be performed independently. In the following, we analyze task τ k , and without loss of generality we focus on an arbitrary job J k of τ k . To simplify presentation, we view an idle processor as executing a conceptually idle task, whose priority is lower than any task in the system.
GSYY focuses on the busy period starting at r k (the release time of the analyzed job J k ), and at each time point in the busy period at least one of the following two conditions holds:
• All processors are busy.

• J k is executing. J k finishes its execution at the end of the busy period. So the target of the analysis is to find the minimal length up to which the busy period is guaranteed to end. The analysis is performed in the following three steps:

1. Deriving a lower bound of the capacity provided by the processing platform in the busy period When the analyzed job instance J k is running, other processors may execute tasks with either higher priorities or lower priorities than τ k . However, since the concrete worstcase behavior of the system is unknown, GSYY assumes that these processors are executing lower-priority tasks when J k is executing, to get a safe lower bound of the processing capacity to accommodate higher-priority tasks. In Figure 1, only the area inside the dashed rectangles is accounted to be useful processing capacity, which is (x -C k ) × M if the length of the busy period is x.

2. Deriving an upper bound of the interference by higher-priority tasks in the busy period GSYY computes an upper bound of the maximal interference of each individual task in the busy period, and uses the sum of them as a safe upper bound of the total interference of all higher-priority tasks. The interference of a higher-priority task τ i is computed in two steps. First, the maximal workload of τ i that may execute in the busy period is computed, then τ i 's interference is the part of its workload that can actually prevent the analyzed job J k from execution.

The workload of a task in a time interval [a, b) can be divided into three parts: It is proved that the critical instant of global fixed-priority scheduling occurs when all higher-priority tasks, except at most M -1 of them, release jobs simultaneously with the release of the analyzed job J k . In other words, at most M -1 higher-priority tasks have carry-in jobs, while all the other higher-priority tasks only have body and carry-out jobs. div.head: B. Pessimism in GSYY
div.p: In the following we discuss the reason why GSYY is pessimistic, which discloses the opportunity for us to improve the analysis precision. For simplicity of explanation, we focus on two tasks τ k-1 and τ k . We will show that when analyzing the response time of τ k , the assumptions made in the calculation of interference of τ k-1 contradicts with the assumptions made in the analysis procedure of τ k-1 . This indicates that impossible behaviors are included in the analysis when the local worst cases in individual analysis steps are composed, which leads to pessimistic response time bound estimation. In the following we explain the contradiction in details.

We first consider the analysis procedure of τ k-1 . Recall that in step 1, only the area in the dashed rectangles of Figure 1 is counted as useful processing capacity to execute higher priority tasks. In other words, the worst-case response time bound R k-1 is computed under the assumption:

I. "All processors are executing tasks with priorities no higher than τ k-1 when τ k-1 is executing." Then we consider the analysis of τ k , where we need to calculate the maximal workload in the busy period of tasks with higher priority than τ k (i.e., tasks with index smaller than k). If τ k-1 has carry-in in the busy period, the maximal workload of each higher priority task is calculated according to Equation (2), assuming that the execution of the carry-in job is performed as late as possible, and finishes exactly at its worst-case response time bound (R k-1 time units after its release time), as shown in Figure 2.

To calculate the response time bound of τ k , the interference of higher-priority tasks are assumed to execute not in parallel with the analyzed job J k of τ k . In other words, only the area in the dashed rectangles of Figure 1 is used to accommodate the interference of τ k-1 . By the definition of the busy period, when J k is not executing, all processors are occupied by tasks with higher priority than τ k . Therefore, the interference of the carry-in job of τ k-1 is counted under the assumption II. "All processors are executing tasks with priorities higher than τ k when the carry-in job of τ k-1 is executing." We can see a contradiction between the two assumptions I and II: when calculating the worst-case workload of τ k-1 , we assume the carry-in job of τ k-1 does not execute in parallel with higher priority tasks; when counting the interference to τ k by the carry-in job of τ k-1 , the worstcase scenario is constructed with the opposite assumption.

div.head: IV. NEW ANALYSIS METHOD
div.p: In this section we address the pessimism of GSYY discussed in last section, and present a new analysis method to better bound the interference of carry-in jobs and thus improve the analysis precision over GSYY. The precision improvement is obtained at the price of a higher complexity of the analysis procedure. We also introduce optimization techniques to improve the efficiency of our new method.

div.head: A. Bounding Carry-In Interference
div.p: We first introduce the key idea of our new method using two tasks τ k-1 and τ k . Later we will introduce how to apply the idea in the general case. We use J ci k-1 to denote the carry-in job of τ k-1 when analyzing the response time of an arbitrary job J k of τ k .

Recall that the response time bound R k-1 of τ k-1 is calculated under the assumption that all processors are occupied by higher-priority tasks τ 1 , • • • , τ k-2 only when τ k-1 is not executing. If J ci k-1 reaches the worst-case response time bound R k-1 , J ci k-1 can only execute in time intervals in which at least one processor, apart from the one executing J ci k-1 , is executing a task with lower priority than τ k-1 . So we can conclude that J ci k-1 must be executing in parallel with the analyzed job J k . Therefore, when calculating the interference of τ k-1 to J k , the workload of J ci k-1 should not be included.

On the other hand, if we include J ci k-1 's workload into the interference to J k , i.e., let J ci k-1 execute when J k is not executing, the response time of J ci k-1 should be smaller than R k-1 . This is because, in this case, J ci k-1 executes in parallel with higher-priority tasks and thus the processing capacity in parallel with its execution can be used to accommodate workload of higher-priority tasks. So the total workload of τ k-1 should be calculated using a potentially smaller value to replace R k-1 in (2). Since Δ(τ i , x, R i ) in ( 2) is nondecreasing with respect to R k-1 , the interference of τ k-1 to J k becomes potentially smaller.

In general, the workload of J ci k-1 may partially execute in parallel with J k , and only the part of its workload not executing in parallel with J k should be counted into the interference. div.head: C. Improving Efficiency
div.p: The improved precision of our new method is at the price of a higher complexity of the analysis procedure:

• For each task τ i , we need to compute the matrix R i , which contains (M -1) × (C i + 1) elements (while GSYY only computes one R i ). • In the iterative calculation procedure of R a,b i , each Δ new (τ i , x) is computed by enumerating all possible ∈ [0, C i ] (while GSYY only considers = 0). Therefore, the computation of R i would be time consuming for tasks when (M -1) × (C i +1) is large. In the following, we introduce two systematical optimization techniques to improve the efficiency of our new analysis method.

Actually, in the above fixed-point iteration procedure, it is sufficient to set the initial value x 0 as any number that is guaranteed to be no larger than the desired solution. A larger initial value would lead to faster convergence of the fixed-point iteration procedure.

For two functions g 1 (x) and g 2 (x), if g 1 (x) is always above g 2 (x), i.e., ∀x : g 1 (x) ≥ g 2 (x), the intersection between g 1 (x) and the diagonal must be no smaller than the intersection between g 2 (x) and the diagonal. If we want to solve both x = g 1 (x) and x = g 2 (x), we can first solve x = g 2 (x), the minimal solution of which can be used as the initial value for solving x = g 1 (x) for potentially faster convergence.

div.head: V. PERFORMANCE EVALUATION
div.p: We evaluate both the precision and efficiency of the our new analysis method with randomly generated task sets, comparing with the state-of-the-art method GSYY.

Task sets are generated by the following strategy. First, a task set of M + 1 tasks is generated. Then we iteratively increase the number of tasks by 1 to generate a new task set. This process is iterated until the normalized total utilization is larger than 1. The whole procedure is then repeated, starting with a new task set of M +1 tasks, until a reasonably large sample space is generated. To generate each task, T i is randomly chosen in a specified range and C i is randomly chosen in [1, T i /2]. All tasks have implicit deadlines, i..e, D i = T i . Task priorities are assigned following the rate monotonic scheme.

div.head: A. Precision
div.p: We first evaluate the improvement of obtained response time bounds by our new method over GSYY. In the experiments of Figure 7, the range of T i for each task τ i is [2,100]. The x-axis denotes the normalized total utilization of the tested task sets, and the two curves are

• imp task denotes the ratio between the number of tasks whose response time bounds are improved and the total number of tasks that are tested (at the target normalized total utilization specified by the x-axis value). • avg imp denotes the average improvement ratio of all tasks whose response time bounds are improved. The improvement ratio of a task is computed by
div.formula: R GSYY -R new R GSYY
div.p: where R GSYY and R new is the response time bound obtained by GSYY and our new method for this task, respectively. • total avg imp denotes the average improvement ratio of all tasks. The response time bound obtained by either method is set to be D i if τ i is decided to be not schedulable by this method. From Figure 7 we can see that our new method has greater improvement over GSYY for task sets with medium normalized total utilization, which is actually the breakdown utilization. As the number of processors increases, the break-down utilization becomes slower, so the utilization range of peak improvement also moves to the lower end.

Figure 8 shows the evaluation results in terms of acceptance ratio in experiments with different number of processors. The acceptance ratio of an analysis method is defined as the ratio between the number of task sets decided to be schedulable by this analysis method and the total number of tested task sets.

The above experiments show that our new method can improve the analysis precision. Although the improvement of acceptance ratio is not very large, the response time bounds obtained by our method is considerably more precise than the state-of-the-art. The response time itself (apart from being used for schedulability analysis) is also an important timing property of interest in many real-time systems. For example, in distributed systems, improvement of local response time on a component may greatly reduce the pessimism of end-to-end performance analysis. Our new method proposed may be used to improve the timing analysis precision of a wide range of real-time systems by providing tighter response time bounds.

div.head: B. Efficiency
div.p: We also evaluate the analysis efficiency of our new method. In Figure 9, the three curves are Then we change the number of processors M . In Figure 9-(b), we set the number of processors as 10, and change the upper limit of C i . We can see that indeed our new method runs slower than GSYY. However, the optimization techniques presented in Section IV-C can significantly improve the analysis efficiency, with which our new method can handle complex task sets in very short time.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we present a new analysis method for global fixed-priority scheduling, to improve the carry-in estimation precision over the existing methods. The key idea is to identify and resolve contradicting (pessimistic) assumptions made in the analysis procedure. The resulting new analysis method improves the analysis precision, but has a higher complexity. We also introduce techniques to optimize our new method for better efficiency. Experiments with randomly generated task sets show that our new method can improve the state-of-the-art analysis method while maintaining reasonable efficiency.

In this paper, the task priorities are assumed to be given by the system designer. However, it has been proved that the system schedulability can be greatly improved by adjusting the priority order of tasks [16], [17]. As future work we will study how to efficiently apply the new analysis method to priority assignment of global fixed-priority scheduling for better schedulability. Another potential future work is to integrate our new method with the limited preemption scheduling paradigm [26], which also generally results in better schedulability than fully-preemptive global scheduling algorithms.
